en: Preface to the Dharma of Vajra-Amṛtakuṇḍalī from the *Dhāraṇī-piṭaka* of the Western Quarter.
In the *Catalogue of Sacred Teachings Newly Sought in Tang by Great Master Jikaku Ennin*,
there is one fascicle titled *The Rite of Amṛtakuṇḍalī*.
It is regrettable that this work was lost within the scriptures and manuals of the Secret (Guhyaka) Section and has not been transmitted.
Annen’s *Hakka hihitsu* (Secret Record of the Eight Houses) states that this dharma was brought [to Japan] at the request of the two masters Saichō and Ennin;
however, it is because Saichō did not actually bring it.
According to the records in the *Yuezhou lu*,
there is a dharma for the Bodhisattva Kumbhīra,
but there is no dharma for Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
Yet the *Biyulu* (Secret Records) does not mention the Bodhisattva-dharma.
Although Anran’s intention was undoubtedly to regard both [the Buddha and the Bodhisattva] as equal,
how can it be that their names have already diverged?
Regarding the Dharma of General Vajramusti Bodhisattva:
it is one of the four miscellaneous maṇḍala ritual manuals transmitted by Saichō;

that is to say, it is nothing other than the "Chapter on the Mantra and Mudrā of the Sovereign Spiritual Power of General Vajramusti Bodhisattva" contained in the eighth fascicle of the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra*.
I fear this is not the Amṛtakuṇḍalī rite that Ennin (Eun-nin) described.
Now, as for Tengan (Teng-an),
his vision was lofty and his discernment far-reaching.
He deeply cherished ancient manuscript scriptures;
his collection was so vast that it was the foremost in the world.
Hundreds of scrolls, with ivory book-marks and yellow silk covers, were arranged upon his shelves.
These are all treasures from the Tang and Sui dynasties, including bronze balances and other artifacts;
there is not one that is not a rare jewel of the world.
It is my good fortune to have been honored with their acquaintance.
Having once obtained his permission,
I opened the kitchen storehouse to examine its contents and happened upon a scroll.
The title reads: "The Dharma of Vajrakumāra Amṛta from within the Western Dhāraṇī-piṭaka.
The character "吒" (zhà) is an error for "荼" (tú).
The internal title is written in formal script as the "Dharma of Kuṇḍalī."
The paper is thin hemp, with red-lacquered rollers, lacking both covers and silk bands;
though it lacks the beauty of elaborate binding,
its ancient fragrance is indeed worth gathering in one's palms.
It is complete from beginning to end;
throughout the entire scroll, there is not a single character that is damaged by insects or illegible.
The brushwork and stroke formations are purely in the calligraphic style of the Tang dynasty.
Thus, ancient and long-lost scriptures of a thousand years' past were encountered unexpectedly in a single day;
so great was my joy and astonishment that I could not contain myself,
and I unrolled them until reaching the end of the scrolls.
The colophon states:

On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Changqing era of the Great Tang, the bhikṣu Haiyun transcribed this record at the East Pagoda Cloister of Qinglong Temple. He respectfully recorded it according to the instructions of his ācārya for future reference and verification. Thus it is concluded.
The calligraphy of the colophon is identical in style to that of the main text.
While the characters are not particularly skillful,
they are orderly and yet possess a sense of vitality.
I then realized that this manuscript written by Haiyun himself was not something transcribed by an ordinary scribe; unconsciously,
I joined my palms and paid homage to it with reverence.
There was a sense that he had met ancient masters face-to-face.
The bhikṣu Haewon was a disciple of Uicheong of Cheongnyongsa, together with Uijin of Dongtaryeon and Beopjeon of Hyeonbosa.
In the eighth year of the Jōwa era, he composed the *Nijū sōjō denbō shidai ki* (Record of the Succession of the Dharma Transmission of the Two Teachings) at Jōjū-ji Temple.
This is the most authoritative source for the bloodline of the masters and disciples of Esoteric Buddhism.
Ennin transcribed this and brought it back to transmit it to our country.
Examining it now based on this,
the "Ācārya" mentioned in the colophon of this scroll refers to Gijo.
There is no doubt that Haewon called himself a śramaṇa who transmitted the teachings through Brahmic script;
it is not difficult to imagine that his mastery of Siddham was unsurpassed.
However, at the beginning of the Changqing era, he still resided with his master at Qinglong Temple.
Yi Cao recited the Sanskrit text,
Haiyun transcribed it,
and they translated this sutra to place it in the East Pagoda Courtyard.
The postscript can serve as sufficient evidence for this.
As for the fact that it is not included in either the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* or the *Zhenyuan Shijiao Lu*,
it must have been produced later.
Furthermore, upon re-examining this fascicle,
there were errors and omissions, as well as redundant characters;
the phrasing was not elegant.
The chapters and sections are disorganized;
the usage of characters in the Sanskrit sounds is chaotic and lacks fixed rules;
and the number of phrases in the dharanis is not annotated.
This is certainly due to the fact that the recorder was not proficient in literary composition.
Although it was unavoidable,
it is clear that the work has not undergone a second revision.
How could it be anything other than a translation of the original?
Ennin arrived in Chang’an in the fifth year of the Kaicheng era and remained there for six years.
He visited the East Pagoda Cloister of Qinglong Temple and beheld various mandalas;
he commissioned the scholar Wang Hui to copy the painted scrolls of the two divisions and transcribed the sutras and commentaries.
He established a hall for making offerings and issued an edict to establish a consecration altar (*abhiṣeka-maṇḍala*) for his own life.
He received the *Garbha-tantra* and the great Dharma of *Susiddhi* from Uijin.
Yizhen provided him with silk for painting scrolls.
Furthermore, he went to Xuangfa Temple to receive the *Garbhadhātu* (Womb Realm) initiation from Faquan.
Faquan bestowed upon him three fascicles each of the *Garbhadhātu-maṇḍala-sūtra* and the ritual manuals for the individual deities.
Furthermore, he studied Siddham under the Tripitaka Master from South India, Ratnacandra, at Qinglong Temple;
these matters are all detailed in the *Record of a Pilgrimage to Seek the Dharma in Tang*.
One might therefore consider that although Haiyun had previously moved to Jingzhu Temple, [he was subsequently invited by Wuzhen].
Furthermore, fearing that [the master] had already passed away,
because Yizhen’s Dharma was entirely identical to that of his own school,
this manuscript was still present at the East Pagoda Cloister at that time.
If the profound Dharma had never been circulated in the world,
it was only natural that Enchin alone obtained it from his master and brought it back,
while it remained untransmitted to other families.
Indeed, this scroll is the very original brought back from abroad;
it is truly a supreme treasure of the "three excellences."
How could its value be merely that of a precious jade tablet?
Were it not for this *Kṣurikā-Mārīcī-Kuṇḍalī* Dharma, it might have been irrevocably lost to the world.
Since that land had already discarded it long ago, it was only fitting that it would ultimately not enter the Tripitaka collection.
Master Qingshan told me: [text continues].
This sutra emerged from Sekizan.
Not long after Kōen brought it back,
Eishu went from Enryaku-ji to Sekizan-ji.
The original transmission of the Tendai Esoteric school was lost;
thereafter, from the Chunyu era onward, no great scholars emerged at Ishiyama,
and the teachings remained confined to high shelves, never again circulating in the world.
It is not at all surprising that works such as the *Aśvaghosa-śāstra* are nowhere to be seen;
the *Juechan-chaoshe* merely mentions their titles without citing their texts,
and it appears that even the masters of the Eastern Esoteric tradition did not transmit them.
Upon reciting it through once,
one immediately recognizes that it belongs to the *Garbhadhātu* (Womb Treasury) system as one of the miscellaneous esoteric scriptures;
its flavor is extremely similar to texts such as the *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha*.
The date of composition of the original Sanskrit manuscript is not far removed from that of the *Saṃyuktāgama*.
Compared with other *Krodharāja Mañjuśrī* dharmas,
this sūtra is the most extensive.
The essence of the altar rituals and the complexity of the methods for accomplishment are such that,
despite my compilation of these scriptures, I dare not venture to encompass them all.
The mudrās and mantras are also most abundant;
it may be said that this represents the ultimate development and preparation of the specific ritual methods for the deity Cundā,
and is something that must not be lacking within the Secret Treasury.
Alas, things likewise experience both meeting and not meeting,
just as it is among human beings;
even if they remain hidden for a long time.
Fortunately spared from the ashes of the kalpa,
these traces remain for a hundred generations;
as for who gains or loses, the fruit of this is truly beyond measure.
He was deeply moved by this and could not remain unmoved;
he therefore requested to borrow it and applied himself to it diligently for ten days.
I have handwritten a copy,
awaiting the conditions for its carving onto printing blocks to be transmitted to future generations.
This is in the third month of this year.
Dr. Oubai Sen’s mother has passed away.
The doctor was exceptionally filial;
he has selected the seventh day after her death as the anniversary for the memorial service.
Desiring to bestow these precious Buddhist scriptures upon my kinsmen and friends to provide merit for their posthumous welfare,
he entrusted me with the task of selecting, collating, and editing them.
I then retrieved them from the bottom of a chest and presented them as a gift.
I have re-examined the text, added headings as a table of contents,
carefully corrected the section breaks and titles,
and made numerous corrections to characters that were misdrawn or otherwise erroneous.
"Entrusting this to the printing blocks so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Thus was it recorded by Mikkyō Matsuji, Ōmura Seihai, on the Buddha’s Birthday in the Great Zheng Bingchen year, beneath the southern window of the Unjikan (The Hut of Non-Conceptualization).

The First Chapter: Introduction to the Rīṭa-Mañjuśrī Dharma.
At that time, the Vajra Bodhisattva, for the benefit of all sentient beings—men, women, boys, and girls—expounded the chapter on the Dharma of Protection.
In the past, when the devas and asuras fought,
from the Four Heavenly Kings up to Śakra Devānām Indra,
all those yakṣas, rākṣasas, and beings of great power [were involved].
They were all utterly defeated and driven back by the army of the asuras;
terrified, they fled in haste until the Heaven of the Thirty-three was shaken throughout.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, along with all the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others dwelling on the earth and in the sky, were likewise moved.
The sun, moon, and stars; the ṛṣis; the wind god; Maheśvara; Vasu; Agni; Varuṇa; all the Rudras; Maheśvara; Nārāyaṇa; Vināyaka, and all the various mantra-deities.
All incantations, poisons, sorcery, and the like;
medicinal arts performed by Vṛhaspati;
and the methods of medicinal arts taught in the Atharvaveda and other such works.
Furthermore, all the dharmas taught by Kharoṭaka and others were completely dispersed as they fought with the asuras;
the asura army achieved great victory and power.
During that period of the kalpa’s turbid and evil age,
sentient beings who cultivate merit will be few,
while those who commit transgressions will be many.
Consequently, the devas diminish while the asuras flourish,
and they cannot be overcome by any incantations, spells, poisons, or medicinal drugs.
At that time, the Buddha-dharma was in decline.
Then the World-Honored One,
with his eyes of compassion, beheld this situation.
He then addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, saying:
"Listen attentively now to all the mantras and incantations of the various devas."
All have been crushed and subdued by the army of the asuras.
By using your majestic spiritual power to rescue the devas now,
you will attain great benefit.
You have been consecrated by all the Buddhas;
you shall attain the supernatural powers of all the great Bodhisattvas and reach the stage of non-retrogression.
I now bestow this prediction of enlightenment upon you in my very presence.
He shall attain Buddhahood,
with the name Tathāgata Immeasurable Supreme Wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajra—
Upon hearing the Buddha’s prophecy, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
Through the Buddha’s empowerment, he immediately transformed himself into the Wrathful Vajra King,
his bodily radiance blazing like a thousand suns.
He immediately entered the Vajra Samādhi and manifested a terrifying form,
endowed with a thousand arms and a thousand eyes, fully possessing majestic power and virtue.
By means of supernatural powers, he manifested emanations that filled the summit of Mount Sumeru and dwelt in the sky—
namely, Vajra-aṅkuśa, Vajra-pāśa, and Vajra-kaṅkaṭa.
Vajratāṭaka, vajracaṇḍīradatta, vajraduṇḍa, vajrayūtha, vajraśekhara, vajramudrī, vajrapāṇi mahāvajra, vajraśreṣṭha.
Rā-vajra-druma-rā-vajra-īśvara-vajra-śara-vajra-muśala-vajra-karāla-vajra-niṣṭhita-vajra-śakti-vajra-śūla-vajra-pāśa.
Vajradhanu-vajra-śūla, vajramāra, and so forth—
such vajras are exceedingly great and terrifying.
It was a manifestation created by all the Buddhas.
At that time, the great beings who witnessed it were all struck with terror and went to Śakra’s abode to tell him.
"Lord of Devas, who is this that has come?
Could it be that the army of the asuras intends to swallow up us gods,
along with the gandharvas, kinnaras, sūryas, vasus, rudras, and other powerful deities who are formidable and most difficult to behold?"
"By the power of this sorcery, we gods have all been deluded and confused.
We pray only that the Lord of Devas will compassionately protect us.
In the past, the Heavenly Lord engaged in battle with the asuras."
By means of ritual methods, he manifested a wrathful and terrifying form to cause them fear,
thereby securing the safety of ourselves and all the devas.
Having thus entreated Śakra,
he further praised him, saying:
"O Great Virtue, Honored One among the Gods, you who are compassionate toward all."
Because of this asura, we repeatedly give rise to afflictions;
though we exhaust all our spiritual powers, we cannot dispel this māra.
We pray only to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings that this enemy may be driven away and scattered.
At that time, after the various devas had praised Śakra,
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva arrived before them and saw that the bodies of all the devas were trembling with fear.
He immediately beheld the true body’s blazing radiance and majestic virtue;
standing before the Lord of Devas, he uttered these words:
"Namo Buddhāya."
When Śakra heard the sound of praising the Buddha,
his heart became peaceful;
he was awakened and alerted by the wisdom of the Buddha.
He immediately paid homage with reverence, prostrated, and made offerings according to the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vajra praised him in verse:
"I bow my head to the Bhagavān, The Wrathful Vajra King."
With a heart of great compassion, having long cultivated the bodhisattva practices,
your body is like the full moon; may you bring us cool relief and protect and assist the hosts of devas by defeating the asuras.
This is certainly the Buddha’s skillful means; Therefore, he manifests this body,
And can further eliminate the evil realms, Rescue suffering sentient beings,
And subdue great yakṣas, Rākṣasas, malevolent nāgas, and the like.
And all the retinues of Māras, he is able to utterly subdue them.
If there are sentient beings who are able to perceive the Dharma-body, their four grave offenses shall be extinguished; I now prostrate with my head at his feet.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having finished praising Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva,
stood to one side.
Then Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva...
Desiring to destroy the army of the asuras,
he immediately transformed into a terrifying form of wrathful anger;
from the four sides of the summit of Mount Sumeru, he manifested vajra-flames that came forth, intending to incinerate them.
When the asura army saw them from afar, they were all struck with fear;
their minds became distressed,
and they immediately scattered and fled.
By the power of the vajra, they could not depart,
nor did they dare to turn back;
they gazed directly at the Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva.
In every place one looks,
one sees the Vajra-deva swallowing all asuras,
grasping the heads of all asuras with his hands.
With his adamantine fangs, he hung countless asuras;
his eyes were like a thousand flashes of lightning,
and his mouth was like a sea of blood.
The hundreds of thousands of millions of asura armies were unable to fill the four sides;
their blood was like great stars, and they then transformed into the terrifying forms of the Mother of Ghosts (Hārītī).
They fled back to join the army of the asuras;
blood flowed across the earth like rivers and seas,
which the great wind blew into surging waves.
Within it, he manifested four sister goddesses who were exceedingly terrifying,
as well as the Bodhisattva Subāhulodra, also known as Mulu.
They all dwell within the great ocean and roam throughout the entire earth.
Furthermore, from within their caves, there emerge countless *uṣṇa*-pretas (heat-ghosts) of most terrifying form.
Furthermore, Kumāra was born;
he immediately led his host of troops and struck the asuras away.
From that time onward.
Within the cave dwellings there arise the *Sagandha*, *Abhasmara*, and *Ummada* spirits.
They are able to manifest various terrifying forms;

they can subdue *asura* women, seize human-fetus ghosts (*pūtanā*), and kill spirits that afflict children. Wandering day and night, they sniff at foul places, suck the vital essence of infants, and drink blood and eat flesh.
Such as these, he is able to utterly subdue;
he also protects Śakra as he defeats the asuras.
At that time, the asura army is shattered into fine dust.
There was no one who turned back.
All the goddesses and gandharva maidens were filled with great joy;
they played various kinds of music, struck celestial drums, scattered heavenly flowers, and offered praises.
Once the army of the asuras had been crushed and the gods had achieved victory,
they all remained filled with wrath, [exclaiming], "Such is the majestic power and authority of the King!"
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, joined his palms,
prostrated at the feet of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva,
and stood before him.
Furthermore, the sons of the gods scattered mandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and sandalwood powder;
they also scattered in the sky immeasurable koṭis of celestial garments, necklaces, and the seven treasures of gold and silver.
Scattered into the heavens, they transformed into precious canopies.
Having made offerings to the Wrathful Kings, they were offered up as palaces and towers within the void; having thus made offerings to the Vajra Bodhisattvas, they paid their respects.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva,
filled with joy and leaping for gladness,
conferred the empowerment upon Śakra.
He immediately descended from the heavens and approached the World-Honored One.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulating him three times,
he addressed him, saying:
Excellent, excellent!
Son of the Buddha, your majestic power, wisdom, and virtue are immeasurable and boundless.
You have now completed your buddha-work.
Because you have brought great benefit to the Buddha’s teachings,
your *dharmakāya* has long since increased in wisdom.
You now possess the mantra methods, the methods of great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*), and the *samaya* methods.
"You should now explain the method for subduing all spirits and deities.

Then, before the Buddha, he spoke of the accomplishment of all worldly mantra-dharmas, saying:

*Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo śrīvajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye. Namo vajrakrodhāya nirdiṣṭapraśastavikṛtavajrakarāya ugradaṃṣṭrotkaṭabhayānakarūpāya asurasuvarakṣarākṣasayakṣaśatrūṇāṃ pramathane śāstāya varakanakavajrāya.*
Vaiḍūrya-laṅkṛta-śrīrāja sarva-nāga-yakṣa-rākṣasa-asura-bhṛta.
piśāca-vijñāna-vināyaka-avattakalataḥ tadanu oṃ amṛta-kumārī-taṇḍali.

*Svāhā*. This is the root great mantra.
It is used when invoking Kuntali, and it is also capable of accomplishing all dharmas.
The *Kundalī Water-Mantra*: *Namaḥ vajra-krodhāya mahākrodha-rājāya amitavāra-prakrama-ya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. Recite this mantra seven times over water and use it to wash the face.
It wards off all *vināyakas*.
The heart-mantra of Cundā: *Namo ratnatrayāya | namo vajrakrodhāya | oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mantra should be constantly maintained.
All undertakings will be successfully accomplished.

The *Krodharāja Cundā* Boundary-binding Mantra: *Namo samantavajrāṇām | Kīra khara ḍaṭa ḍaṭa maṭa maṭa paṇḍa paṇḍa sarvān uṣṭrān yakṣān rākṣasān nārakṣasān saṃtati-ujjñāna-śyanda-smara-paṇḍa-kulu-samantavajriṇa | Kuru kuru amale vimale kuru namaye unaya unaya vara vara kara kara smara paṇḍami jvala jvala amṛta-cuṇḍali hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.* Recite this mantra over water, or over ashes, or over white mustard seeds seven times; with these consecrated substances, bind the boundary.
It wards off all vināyakas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, mad spirits, piśācas,
and all those who create obstacles, so that they cannot cause disturbance or affliction.

The *Kundali* Body-Protection Mantra: *Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo vajrakrodhāya. Oṃ amṛta-kundali kṣa kṣa mama sarvasattvānāṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.* Recite this mantra seven times to protect the body and bind the boundary (*sīmābandha*).
Success is immediately attained.

The *Samaya-mantra* of Kuṇḍalī: *Namo ratnatrayāya | namo vajrapāṇaye | oṃ amṛtakuṇḍali kha kha kha kha kha kha kha huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.* This mantra is for entering the maṇḍala.
It is named the Samādhi that Accomplishes All Deeds.

The mantra for the offering to Kuṇḍalī is: Namo ratnatrayāya | Oṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave jike jike vimale vimale vireye vireni hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. With this mantra, all offering substances are to be consecrated seven times.
No ghosts or spirits shall be able to create obstacles or difficulties.

The *Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa* mantra for the offering of *gaṇacakra*: *Namaḥ ratnatrayāya | namaḥ vajrakrodhāya | oṃ amṛtakuṇḍali hana hana hara hara āle āle huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the method of this mantra.
Take a copper bowl and fill it with pure water.
Take *gulu* grass and various flowers and scatter them into the water.
Recite the mantra seven times as an offering.
All that is undertaken shall be accomplished.

The mantra for burning incense for Kuṇḍalī is: *Namo ratnatrayāya | namo vajrakrodhāya | oṃ amṛte cira-cira sva-ma-nu-śeṇi hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Recite this mantra seven times over the incense to be burned and the unguents.
Thereafter, perform the offering.

For the *mantra* for offering food and drink to Kuntali: *Namo ratnatrayāya*. *Namo śrīvajrapāṇaye*. *Oṃ amṛte hahara varivariṇi svāhā*. Recite this *mantra* seven times over all the food as an offering.
The ritual action is complete.

For the mantra for causing [a deity] to descend into speech: *Namo ratnatrayāya*. *Namo mahākrodharājāya*. *Oṃ amṛta-kumārī jambhaya stambhaya jambhaya stambhaya*. Regarding this mantra method, if one intends to cause someone to speak [through possession], one should recite it seven times over water or white mustard seeds.
Scatter [the flowers] before him and burn incense; he will immediately give his response.
The mantra of Mañjuśrī for binding is: *Namo ratnatrayāya, namo mañjughoṣāya, oṃ amṛte muñca muñca hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Recite this mantra over the flowers once, or over the water once.
If the spirits manifest before one's face, one should immediately answer them.
Alternatively, by uttering the sound "HŪṂ," they will be dispelled.

The *maṇtra* for dispatching the spirits of Muṇḍarī is as follows: *Namo ratnatrayāya | namo ścaṇḍavajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye amitājetigamana-vegavate amṛteje cche cche vidyādhararāja kumāri je thaḥ svāhā svabhāvānāṃ svāhā.* If one recites this *maṇtra* seven times while burning incense, the ghosts and spirits will be immediately dispatched.

The Mantra for Kuntali’s Method of Donning Armor: *Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo vajrakrodhāya. Oṃ amṛtakuṇḍali kuṇḍala mama sarvāyurvaineyaka-vajra hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.* If this mantra is recited seven times, one immediately succeeds in donning the armor.
The *Muṇḍarī-cūḍābandhana-mantra*: Oṃ amṛta muṇḍarī kṣa kṣa mama hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Recite this mantra seven times.

Tie the hair on the crown of the head into a single knot. If protecting companions, use the mantra for *kuśa* grass and the method for wearing it; this same mantra is also used for all methods of universal protection.

Then, recite the root mantra to invite Kuntali, so that the ritual of the mantra may be swiftly accomplished. Furthermore, recite the incense mantra, the *āgama* mantra, and the offering mantra, reciting each seven times in succession as an offering.
One shall attain the extinction of all sins and acquire immeasurable merit;
all undertakings shall be brought to fulfillment,
and all evils shall be eliminated.
One attains entry into the Samaya-maṇḍala.

To establish the efficacy [of the rite], recite the *Muṇḍarī-bādhana-mantra*: *Namo ratnatrayāya | namo ścañcabajrapāṇaye mahāvīraparākramāya vajrāṅkāratanapuṣṇāya mārī muṇḍarīrādharāya mahābhīṣaṇavaruṇadhāriṇe krodharājāya samanta-* [Recite this mantra.]
Vajraśvara viṣphuliṅgāṭa hoṣa sambhrama mudrāsvanakarāya tadyathā.
Oṃ amṛta-kuṇḍali tura tura.
Yuru yuru juru juru muru muru.
Hulu hulu muhu muhula kulu kulu.
traṭa traṭa maṭa maṭa kaṭe kaṭe
dhaka dhaka duna duna viduna.
Anaye anaye bhadra bhadra bhadre bhadre.
Oṃ he amīṣa amīṣa parāmīṣa parāmīṣa.

Iṭṭamānuṣaśarīre hiriḍḍhamā hiriḍḍhaṃ vaṇattha maṇattha jñāmba pabba jñāmba pabba nirdiyapabba rolapabba pabbata utthapabba hasahasa pabba lūnadi kirodapabba ukkulusa ukkulusa vikulusa vikulusa akulusa akulusa akulusa pabhānahana dhahapacchataṭṭha visayaṃ chaṃchaṃ pabhagavantam amitākuṇḍali kha kha svāhā. This mantra, when recited, swiftly attains its efficacy.
First, one must perform offerings.
At each session, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Thereafter, select the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
According to another version, on the twenty-third, twenty-fourth, the ninth day, and the final day of the month,
one shall abstain from food for one day and one night.
Having bathed with purity and put on new, clean garments.
Taking various kinds of incense, flowers, food, drink, and fruits,
one should offer them before the image according to one's capacity and the season.
Then, with palms joined, prostrate to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
If one wishes to bind a man, a woman, a boy, or a girl, one should recite the mantra seven times while burning agallochum incense;
this applies regardless of whether they are ill or healthy.
They were all completely bound.
Whether it was turning over an alms bowl, a bamboo joint, a pillar, a jar, or a pestle,
or even turning over a kalpa-vṛkṣa tree.
Or, while looking at an object in a mirror or looking up at one's own thumb,
perform all actions while burning agalloch incense and reciting the mantra once or seven times.
All shall attain their wishes.
If one desires to treat illnesses caused by ghosts, demons, or wild paths,
as well as to protect oneself and others, [one should do so].
Subduing all nāgas to beg for rain or to stop it, and to eliminate calamities;
as well as bringing about peace, security, and abundance;
subduing bandits and banishing enemies.
It subdues all poisons, evil lightning, and violent winds,
as well as yellow insects that devour crops;
it is also capable of taming all wicked people and malevolent spirits.
It can also retrieve all hidden treasures and enter the caves of the asuras;
it can cause others to reconcile,
and it can also cause others to harbor mutual hatred, be driven away, or depart.
It can also dispel all that lacks majesty and power,
and it can cause the merit and virtue of all people to be perfected;
it accomplishes all dharmas that are performed.
One should burn agalloch incense throughout.
This mantra is capable of performing hundreds of thousands of supreme rites.
It reaches all those who have seen the Buddha, as well as Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, the various bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
It can extinguish all sins,
attain great wealth and nobility,
and achieve great respect among all sentient beings.
One will also attain great dhāraṇī-retention;
one will also be able to eliminate all fears;
and one will also be able to eliminate famine.
They are able to benefit all sentient beings;
they possess long life and freedom from illness;
their eloquence is perfected, and they have many attendants.
Their storehouses overflowed;
their commercial ventures yielded great profit;
and they served the king with such success that he was filled with joy.
If one enters a military formation,
or engages in combat, dispute, or gambling, one shall emerge victorious in all cases. Furthermore,
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharmas will all be accomplished.
Chapter Two: The Method for Selecting the Site. Furthermore, regarding the method for accomplishing the mandala site, one must first be able to select that location.
One should stay near the bank of a pure river,
or at a place where two rivers converge,
upon a level expanse of sand.
Either near the edge of a pond,
or in mountain forests, in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka), or in empty, secluded groves;
or within empty, secluded shrines to the gods.
Either in a śītavana cemetery,
or within a monastery,
or before a stūpa containing relics.
Alternatively, one may take a beautiful bird that makes sounds pleasant for people to hear from a place abundant with various flowers;
such a location is also suitable.
It is also permissible to stay at a place where a herd of deer resides.
However, if there are hawks, falcons, old crows, owls,
*kumbhāṇḍas*, wild magpies, horned owls, jackals, or other such birds and beasts dwelling within that forest, then such a place is not suitable for use.
It should be near a riverbank where that river has clear water flowing full within its pools,
and where clear water overflows the banks.
Alternatively, it may be obtained on the shores of the ocean at places praised by all Buddhas,
or at sites where there are ancient traces of the Noble Ones.
If one obtains such a location, [one should proceed].
That method will quickly succeed.
Then, clear the ground of its tiles, rubble, bricks, bones, stones, hair, and charcoal.
If one sees within it foul mud, excrement, cesspools, pits, or ancient tombs, [one must remove them].
If one sees such things, they are also of no use.
If these are absent,
take good yellow earth and pile it up to make it level.
If, while performing the ritual of clearing the ground, an inauspicious sign appears, it is not suitable to proceed;
one should take [the site] only when an auspicious sign appears.
Even if neither sign appears, one may still take it.
If in the four directions there is a beautiful bird, red as the color of fire, seen perched upon a tree;
or if it sits upon a tree with beautiful and exquisite flowers and fruits, or upon a sprouting branch, this is auspicious and shall cause the rite to be accomplished.
Furthermore, it is not auspicious for one to sit upon or dwell in the hollows of withered and evil trees;
even if a bird comes there and utters cries of fear or makes harsh sounds, it is likewise not to be used.
If one performs rites for subduing enemies,
the aforementioned evil places will cause those rites to be swiftly accomplished.
If one performs rites for auspiciousness, [the same applies].
If one obtains such an excellent location, one will immediately achieve accomplishment.
Furthermore, it is said again:
if a jackal or a fox finds a wretched place such as thorns, sand, or a mound of earth.
One obtains all results for the rites for subduing enemies.
If there are tigers, lions, or white elephants, it is auspicious to perform rites for prosperity.
However, if the wind is too violent, [it is not so].
If one produces evil sounds that cause people to fear,
or creates smoke, mist, hail, fierce winds, rain, and black dust—
such places are used when performing malevolent rites.
If there is an easterly-southerly wind or a westerly-northerly wind,
performing rites for auspiciousness will not bring good fortune;
one who acts in such a manner will meet with misfortune.
The mantra-practitioner should perform this with careful reflection.
Chapter Three: The Mandala for the Accomplishment of Kuntali. Furthermore, regarding the method for establishing the mandala for accomplishment:
First, one must bathe and don fresh, clean garments.
Refrain from harsh speech and false speech.
Toward all sentient beings, give rise to a mind of benefit and compassion, free from any sense of fear.
Those whose bodies do not tremble with fear, who possess wisdom and skillful means, who are unstained by unwholesome dharmas,
who have the aspiration for the Path,
and who have received the Three Refuges.
Always wear clean, fresh, and pure white garments;
make offerings to the Triple Gem;
and constantly recite auspicious mantras and boundary-binding mantras.
Perform the rite of service and offering.
Constantly recite the heart-mantra of Kuṇḍalī one thousand and eight times.
Always sit upon *kuśa* grass before the Vajra.
Consume the three kinds of white foods— non-glutinous rice, milk, and curd—
and perform the preliminary rites; then, facing east, sit and recite the root mantra while invoking [the deity].
Burn aloeswood incense and guggulu incense;
prepare *āgama-dharma* perfumed water and place it before the image;
light one hundred lamps.
Offer food and other necessities according to what one's means permit;
recite the mantra for one day and one night without fail.
Behold Mañjuśrī;
even if there are sounds of thunder or of great terror in the southern direction,
the practitioner of mantras should not give rise to a mind of fear.
Nor is it necessary to look toward the south;
simply, upon hearing [the voice], arise and prostrate to Vajrasattva,
holding a censer in your hand.
One should pay homage to the pure lands of the Buddhas of the four directions and cultivate a mind of making offerings.
If the mantra-practitioner hears voices to their left or right exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! Great Bodhisattva! [one should know that this is a sign of success].
Your dhāraṇī practice has been accomplished;
whatever your mind intends shall be achieved according to your wish.
From this point forward...
One will immediately attain skillful accomplishment in all ritual actions;
through the empowerment of the mantra-deities,
one shall be named an Ācārya.
They attain all that is to be accomplished and their place of abiding;
they attain all forms of reverence in every place of abiding they achieve;
and they are worthy of receiving great offerings from all the world.
It is able to rescue all sentient beings from their suffering and affliction,
and serves as a place of reliance for all sentient beings.

It protects against all difficulties such as yakṣas, rākṣasas, mad spirits, spirits of malevolent sorcery, ḍākinīs, spirits that raise corpses through poisoning, and perils from kings, thieves, water, fire, and magical fetters.
The calamities of gambling and contentious debate; the calamities of great and small thieves; the calamities of famine and perilous mountains with their malevolent birds and beasts;
the calamities of evil winds, thunder, hail, lightning, and thunderbolts; the calamities of malignant stars and all manner of strange portents; and the calamities of all diseases, rivers, and oceans.
In these difficult circumstances,
the mantra-practitioner is able to protect all sentient beings,
causing them to attain intelligence, wisdom, the power of retention (*dhāraṇī*), and eloquence.
A single act of karma can swiftly bring fulfillment;
let the mantra-practitioner not speak falsely.
This can destroy all malevolent incantations.
The mantra-practitioner should know that such immeasurable powers as these are attained.
Furthermore, I shall now explain the ritual for the five kinds of accomplishment maṇḍalas.
The method for examining and selecting the site is as described in the preceding chapter.
One should take a cord and measure thirty-two cubits on all four sides; the stakes should be six feet or one finger-breadth deep.
Then, one must remove the inferior soil, such as tiles, gravel, bones, stones, and the like.
Take yellow earth and firmly compact it until it is level.
Measure it again;
if one proceeds according to the original ritual procedure, success will be attained.
If the dimensions are not according to the traditional standards, the ritual procedure will not be accomplished.
Generally, all mandalas are of three types:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior is the altar of the king;
the middling is the altar of the queen, the crown prince, and the prime minister;
the inferior is the altar of all sentient beings.
That mandala may be constructed either when the sun is setting or during the night;
the upper mandala measures thirty-two cubits.
The middle altar is sixteen cubits,
or eight cubits;
the lower altar is four, two, or one cubit.
If the ritual conditions are not met, it will not be accomplished even if one attempts to perform it.
If one treats a disease involving a spirit that is not permitted to receive a mandala, one must not construct a mandala for them.
However, if it is appropriate to construct a mandala, one should immediately prepare a mandala measuring two cubits.
If it cannot be made to measure one cubit, one must not do so either.
The practitioner of mantras should understand this method for constructing the maṇḍala.
Furthermore, I shall now further explain the ritual for the maṇḍala of the Vajra family.
That maṇḍala is sixteen cubits square and is drawn with powders of five colors.
Open four gates on the altar and install a painted image within it,
as previously described.

One should offer flowers, incense, floral garlands, unguents, sandalwood incense, aloeswood incense, *nāgakesara* incense, dragon-whisker incense, clove, cinnamon, and all other types of incense and flowers.
According to one's capacity, prepare various kinds of food and drink, fruits, ghee, oil, honey, sugar, milk porridge, and curd-rice;
with such fragrant flowers and offerings, worship the Buddha.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is likewise.
After the Vajra Messengers have consumed the three kinds of white foods and the three kinds of sweet foods as an offering,
the one reciting the mantra shall bathe three times a day.
Wearing three kinds of white garments,
one shall abstain from food for one day and one night,
and sit upon a mat of bundled grass before the image in the full lotus posture.
Recite the Great Mantra to invite Kuṇḍalī;
recall him and take agallochum and aloeswood incense to burn as an offering.
Then, prostrate to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Prostrate with palms joined, settle the mind in concentration,
and give rise to a heart of compassion and joy.
Having generated such a state of mind, recite the Great Heart Mantra of Kuṇḍalī one thousand and eight times.
When the recitation of the mantra is completed,
the painted image immediately moves and speaks,
and the true body manifests.
Whatever one desires shall be attained in full perfection.
This is the ritual of the maṇḍala for supreme accomplishment;
the practitioner of mantras should contemplate it well.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the method for accomplishing the painted image:
take white cotton cloth or high-quality silk, ensuring the threads are not cut or broken.
The painter must maintain purity through fasting and the observance of precepts.
In the colored pigments, glue must not be mixed.
Use colors such as saffron, turmeric, red sandalwood, realgar, and azure malachite.
In the center, paint the Buddha.
Seated in the vajra posture,
his body is golden in color;
he wears a light that radiates from his entire body and displays the mudrā of preaching the Dharma.
His left hand, bestowing fearlessness, reaches down to his knee.
To the left of the Buddha, one should paint Vajramañjuśrī,
manifesting a terrifying appearance.
In his upper right hand he holds a vajra;
the next hand grasps a battle-axe;
the lower hand holds a sword.
Next, hold the pusher with the hand;
the left hand holds the lasso;
next, hold the wedge with the lower hand.
Next, one hand holds a wheel;
next, one hand holds a staff,
upon which two eyes are placed.
With both hands joined in *añjali* at the heart,
the eyes are slightly reddish,
and the fangs protrude.
His hair bristles upward like the color of flames.
His entire body is clothed in the radiance of fire, and his form is adorned with various kinds of necklaces.
He bites his lower lip with his upper lip.
The Buddha stands facing forward with his feet treading upon a blue lotus flower.
To the Buddha's right, one should paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
with both hands hanging down to his knees.
He wears a flower crown upon his head;
his hair is yellow,
like the filaments of a lotus.
One should wear the image of Amitābha Buddha upon one’s head.
The clothing and adornments are exactly as described in the Dharma taught by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Above the Buddha image, one should paint two rishis.
Wearing a flower crown and jeweled necklaces,
they scattered flowers over the Buddha.
Beneath the image, one should paint seven-jeweled flowers covering the entire ground.
Having thus completed the painting of the image,
one should immediately place it within the altar.
Take flower incense and unguent incense to make offerings.
Circumambulate seven times,
prostrate, and recite the Dharmadhātu-mantra.
Recite the mantra over white mustard seeds seven times and scatter them in the four directions, above, and below;
then the Vināyakas and various yakṣas will be unable to create obstacles.
All that is performed shall attain the most sublime and supreme accomplishment.
Chapter Four: The Great Dharma of Accomplishment of Kuṇḍalī. Furthermore, the method for accomplishing the supreme great maṇḍala is now explained.
One should select a pure place for forest retreat (āraṇya),
such as before a stūpa containing relics,
or within the gate of a monastery.
Construct an altar four finger-widths high;
smear the ground with fragrant mud and scatter flowers.
Burn acacia wood to kindle the fire.
Take rice blossoms mixed with honey, curd, and white mustard seeds;
recite the heart-mantra of Kuṇḍalī over each one as you burn them,
completing one thousand and eight repetitions.
Then all lands will attain peace and stability;
all malevolent stars and portents will be extinguished, and one will be able to benefit all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is another method:
For one who wishes to benefit all sentient beings,
there is the single-wheel mandala;
within that mandala, a single wheel is installed.
It may be fashioned from gold, or from iron or silver;
one recites the mantra until the wheel begins to turn.
Holding it in one's hand, one enters the ranks;
even the celestial deities dare not oppose them.
One shall attain great wealth and nobility, and be revered by kings.
If one does not waver or shift,
one should recite the mantra continuously until smoke emerges from the hand; having attained this, one shall hold the rank of a Rāja.
He destroys all enemies,
nurtures the myriad people,
and possesses great majestic power.
Furthermore, there are those of great power and abundant wisdom who do not employ the method of smoke.
Recite further until flames emerge;
grasping them with your hand, you will immediately fly up into the void and become a king among the mantra-siddhas.
In this same manner, one should also fashion swords, triple-pronged spears, tridents, vajras, and so forth; by doing so,
one will achieve accomplishment— this is the supreme method.
Furthermore, there is another method:
for one who desires to attain great learning, supreme wisdom, and intelligence,
one should take high-quality *achyranthes aspera* (chángpú).
Having installed [the deity] within the maṇḍala,
one recites the mantra until the three signs appear and it begins to move; then,
one immediately attains the power of dhāraṇī upon hearing it.
Possessing great majesty and eloquence,
all who see him will revere him;
he can recite one thousand [verses] in a single day.
If one does not perceive the sign of smoke,
then even until the flames emerge,
upon taking and eating [the smoke], that [being] will immediately become invisible.
One may go wherever one wishes and attain the status of a king among the invisible ṛṣis,
by the power of the Triple Gem.
One shall attain the accomplishment of these most supreme methods of accomplishment.

Chapter Six: The Section on the Fire-Sacrifice (Homa) Method. Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo ścitana-vajrapāṇaye.
Mahāyakṣa-kṣepanapradaye mahā-bhīra-vāruṇapadaye tadyathā.
Oṃ amṛta-kuṇḍali hulu hulu.
Mulu mulu julu julu tululu tululu.
Mulu mulu karakara kili kili.
Kuru kuru dhuru dhuru huru huru.
Kara kara hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ.
Svāhā nairṛtyebhyaḥ svāhā nāgebhyaḥ.
Svāhā asurebhyaḥ svāhā.
Mālutānāṃ svāhā rutānām.
Svāhā huluhulūbhyah svāhā.
To the gandharvas, svāhā;
to the kiṃnaras.
Svāhā mahoragebhyaḥ svāhā.
To the yakṣas, svāhā;
to the rākṣasas.
Svāhā bhṛtyebhyaḥ svāhā.
To the piśācas, svāhā;
to the kaṭapūtanas.
Svāhā to the bhūtanās; svāhā!
Kakudapūtanebhyaḥ svāhā,
śṛṅgāṭebhyaḥ.
Svāhā apasmārāṇāṃ svāhā.
Cayeṇa svāhā ummadhānaḥ.

Svāhā mahākālāya svāhā.
Cili cili nana svāhā śmaśānapāśinīnām.
Svāhā kāpaparigaye svāhā.
mahākāparikāparikāye svāhā kāpanīye.
Svāhā mahākāparṇaye svāhā.
oṃ ucchuṣmaye svāhā ucchuṣmīṇām.
Svāhā śavariye svāhā.
Śavarāṇa svāhā mahāśavarāṇa.
Svāhā hārītyai svāhā.
Śāṅkariye svāhā mātaṅgakiye.
Svāhā hrīḥ ye svāhā.
Gandhārye svāhā cāṇḍālye.
Svāhā jaṅgulyai svāhā.
Kumārīṇīye svāhā. Namo mahāvajrapāṇaye.
Tadyathā: oṃ amṛta-kumāra hūṃ hūṃ siddhyantu mantrapadāni svāhā. This mantra is for the rite of burning fire.
It can extinguish all calamities,
provide great protection for sentient beings,
and bring peace and stability to them.
Furthermore, there is another method.
For one who desires to attain security and stability,
one should take wood from the mulberry or the *gou* tree.
Both should be twelve finger-widths long.
Recite the mantra once.
Take ghee and honey and mix them together.
Place two pieces of wood at either end;
recite the mantra once and cast one [piece] while calling out the person's name.
Cast it into fire and burn it one thousand and eight times;
then one will immediately attain peace and security.
Furthermore, there is another method:
if one wishes to attain wealth and nobility,
take mulberry wood and all kinds of seeds, and mix them together.
Recite the mantra once for each incense offering.
When one thousand and eight repetitions are completed,
one will immediately attain wealth and nobility.
This rite is applicable to all people.
Furthermore, there is another method:
if one wishes to cause others to feel respect and affection, [one should perform this].
Take white sandalwood incense;
recite the mantra once for each piece burned,
until one thousand and eight repetitions are completed.
One will immediately gain the love and respect of all people.
Furthermore, regarding another method:
if one wishes to cause others to feel fear, [one should perform this rite].
Take agarwood;
recite the mantra once for each incense stick and burn them until one thousand and eight repetitions are complete.
One will immediately attain a serene and joyful countenance.
Furthermore, there is another method:
if one wishes to obtain the physical marks of wealth and nobility.
Take lotus flowers;
recite the mantra once for each flower and burn them one by one,
repeating this one thousand and eight times.
One will immediately attain abundance.
Furthermore, there is another method:
if one wishes to obtain wealth and honor, and for gold, silver, and riches to increase.
Take wood from the little finger [of a corpse] to kindle a fire.
Take powdered gold and powdered silver, mix them with clarified butter (*sarpis*), and burn them.
One will immediately attain wealth and nobility.
All people will fear one who possesses majestic power,
and one shall immediately obtain all manner of wealth and treasures.
Furthermore, there is another method:
If one wishes to cure all malevolent spirits and epileptic spirits,
take black sesame seeds mixed with white mustard seeds and burn them;
they will then be eliminated and cured.
Furthermore, there is another method:
if one wishes to eliminate all hailstones,
one should take branches of the pomegranate tree.
Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and strike the air;
immediately, [the affliction] will be eliminated at that very moment.
Furthermore, there is another method.
If one wishes to subdue a malevolent nāga,
one should take a piece of khadira wood or red sandalwood twelve finger-widths in length.
One should fashion a vajra;
if one desires it to be of the most excellent quality,
one should use iron, brass, red copper, or silver.
As for those mentioned above,
one need only take a single color;
thus, one attains [realization] without requiring so much.
For the purpose of protecting the person of the mantra-practitioner, and for the purpose of subduing evil nāgas, spirits, and deities. Chapter Seven:
The Rituals for Begging Rain and Stopping Rain; The Seventh Chapter on the Rituals for Begging Rain and Stopping Rain by Kuṇḍalī. Furthermore, there is another method:
If one wishes to obtain rain,
one should go to the edge of a pond inhabited by nāgas, or to a place where two rivers meet,
or upon a sandy bank therein, or beside a lotus pond.

Chapter 18: The Ritual of Mudrās. Regarding the ritual of the mudrās of Kṣetrapāla, furthermore, the method of mudrās is explained within the Vajra family of teachings.
There are one hundred and eight great mudrās;
I shall now briefly explain sixteen of them for the sake of the methods of accomplishment.
1. Requesting the Buddha’s Seal: First, join both palms at the heart;

The tips of the two middle fingers touch one another.
Each of the two index fingers presses against the back of the first joint of its respective middle finger.
The two thumbs are bent to press down upon the upper joints of the ring fingers; this is it.
The mantra practitioner, with a joyful countenance, shall place the mudrā upon his crown;

This is called the method of the Sealing of Settling the Mind (Anxin Yin).

travels through the sky, and becomes invisible; furthermore,
one desires to behold the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If one wishes to cause others to love and revere them, to accomplish the most supreme dharmas,
to become widely learned,
and to achieve success in all mantra-dharmas and intelligence;
If one wishes to restrain the prohibitions against others' dharmas, water, fire, and all poisons;
if one wishes to extinguish all *gū* (sorcery), medicinal poisons, and venomous insects;
and if one performs all rites while reciting this Great Heart Mantra (*mahācitta-mantra*), one will immediately attain accomplishment.
This dharma must never be given to one with whom you have no prior acquaintance; however,
it may be given to one who can recite it with a sincere heart.
If one is coarse in conduct, do not give it to them;
if one truly practices with diligence, give it to them;
if one acts with deceit, do not give it to them.
If one speaks the truth, is free from deceit and crookedness, possesses a gentle mind, acts with equanimity,
and receives and honors [the teaching] with faith and love— only to such a person may it be transmitted;
otherwise, do not transmit it.
Next, another method for reciting mantras will be explained separately.
This must not be given to others;
even in death, one must die together with this dharma.
One must certainly not give it to others.
However, one may give it to another person who possesses a good affinity for the Dharma with whom one may exchange it,
or to another who serves and makes offerings to one.
Or those who bestow many precious treasures.
These three kinds of people together are worthy of receiving this Dharma. Why is that?
In order to eliminate stinginess,
this Dharma— the Great Secret Heart-Dharma of Vajra-Ḍāka—
is empowered by all the Buddhas.
It is revered by all the devas;
it can purify and eliminate all manner of transgressions,
and it can subdue all vināyakas.
He is venerated by yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, unmādās, skandās, mātṛs, and gaṇamātṛs.
This mantra-holder attains great merit.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family recites, receives, upholds, and makes offerings to it—
whether writing it themselves or instructing others to write it and then installing and making offerings to it— they shall likewise attain such merit.
Either install it within the house,
or install it upon the estate,
or install it at one of the six places for raising livestock.
Whether it be established in an araṇya,
or at a place of practice such as among the mountains or beneath trees— in all such cases,
one should carry it along and make offerings to it.
All shall provide protection;
in all places there shall be abundance,
and all necessities of life shall be fully provided.
If it is placed atop the house of an elder,
no illnesses or pains shall be able to reach it,
nor shall people be possessed by epileptic spirits.
Fire cannot burn it;
water cannot drown it;
thieves cannot steal it.
The king cannot seize it;
all manner of illnesses are forever absent,
and one attains victory over verbal disputes and contention.
One shall increase immeasurable merit;
in every birth one shall attain the knowledge of past lives,
and upon the end of life, one shall be reborn in the heavens.
They shall never be separated from the Three Jewels.
If they are born among humans,
they will attain great wealth and nobility, as well as intelligence, wisdom, and long life.
One will attain the respect and affection of all;
physical strength and vitality will be abundant;
and one will constantly obtain the benefit of all necessities of life.
There will be immeasurable thousands of myriads of servants and officials,
and kings will pay him respect.
If anyone upholds, recites, reads, copies, or makes offerings to it, [they shall likewise receive such honors].
One shall obtain such immeasurable rewards of merit.
If there are elders, merchant leaders, noble brahmins, or kṣatriyas who have received consecration,
they will believe in and revere this Dharma.
One should perform the offerings as previously explained in the Chapter on the Mandala and enter the samaya.
Such persons shall attain immeasurable merit that is impossible to exhaust;
they will be taken into the care of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
One attains the state of non-retrogression, *avaivartika*;
all Buddhas behold one’s person and provide protection;
and one gains great power and diligence.
No enemies whatsoever shall be able to harm them;
the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi will constantly follow and protect the practitioner,
and all devas and spirits shall always attend to their defense.
One shall attain great wealth and nobility;
whatever aspirations one has in mind shall be fulfilled,
just as previously described.
All powers and praises shall be obtained by the reciter,
as well as the supreme accomplishment for those who enter the maṇḍala.
Having finished preaching this Dharma, all the devas, spirits, and others believed, accepted, and practiced it.

This *Vajrakula-Amṛtakuṇḍalī-dharmaparyāya*, from within the Western Dhāraṇī-piṭaka, in one fascicle, was transcribed and recorded on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Chángqìng era of the Great Táng, at the East Pagoda Cloister of Qīnglóng Monastery, by the Bhikṣu Hǎiyún. It was written in accordance with the instructions of the Ācārya for the purpose of recording it for future reference and for verification. On the twelfth day of the eighth month of the first year of the Taishō era, based on the original manuscript in Hǎiyún’s own hand preserved by Count Kōken Tanaka, this transcription was completed after one proofreading. Recorded by the Layman Shikishin, Ōmura Seihai.
